title: Pitch to a plant manager: replace three aging relay panels with one PLC
summary: A persuasive plant-manager pitch to collapse three aging relay panels into one PLC — with example downtime and cost numbers clearly labeled as examples.

blocks.title: Three relay panels → one PLC
blocks.body: Riverbend Packaging's Line 2 still runs on three aging relay panels from different decades. This pitch asks for budget to replace them with a single PLC platform — not because relays are morally wrong, but because the failure mode is now spare-parts archaeology.

blocks.title: Numbers below are EXAMPLES
blocks.body: Downtime hours, dollar figures, and spare lead times are illustrative for a fictional plant. They are not a quote, not Riverbend's real books, and not a promise. Replace them with your measured historian data before any real capital request.

items.label: EXAMPLE unplanned downtime last quarter tied to relay faults
EXAMPLE lead time on obsolete relay skus

blocks.heading: Why this quarter
blocks.body: The panels still run. That is the trap. Each nuisance fault trains the crew to "tap the contactor" instead of instrumenting the root cause. Meanwhile the vendor for Panel C's ice-cube relays already lists several skus as last-time-buy. Waiting for a catastrophic failure turns a planned project into a weekend scramble with premium labor.

nodes.title: Keep field devices
nodes.detail: Sensors and actuators stay; re-land on new terminals.

nodes.title: One PLC + I/O
nodes.detail: Sequence logic centralized; safety stays hardwired or on a safety PLC per policy.

nodes.title: HMI for faults
nodes.detail: Named alarms instead of which-coil-is-buzzing theater.

nodes.title: Staged cutover
nodes.detail: Weekend windows with rollback — same discipline as any relay-to-PLC migration.

blocks.heading: EXAMPLE cost frame (not a quote)
rows: Depends on brand standards already in the plant
Because panels always hide a surprise
blocks.caption: Replace every cell with vendor quotes and your maintenance ledger before presenting upstairs.

columns.name: Downtime avoided
columns.detail: If EXAMPLE 14 h/quarter at EXAMPLE $2,500/h contribution continues, the project pays for itself in a few quarters — only if your historian agrees.

columns.name: Spare-parts risk
columns.detail: Obsolete relays are a silent balance-sheet risk. One hard-to-get coil can cost more than a weekend of planned work.

columns.name: Diagnosability
columns.detail: Named faults shorten MTTR. That benefit is real even when the dollar model is conservative.

items.label: Scope creep into mechanical rebuilds
items.detail: This pitch is controls. Keep mechanical separately funded.

items.label: Safety circuit mishandling
items.detail: E-stops and guard doors stay compliant — not "absorbed" casually into standard PLC outputs.

items.label: Tribal knowledge loss
items.detail: Budget documentation and shadowing; the relay puzzles in people's heads must become comments and prints.

items.label: Optimistic downtime savings
items.detail: Call examples examples. Measure before promising ROI.

items.title: Survey & prints
items.detail: Ring out existing panels; freeze scope.

items.title: Build & shop test
items.detail: New panel dry-tested before the line sees it.

items.title: Cut sequence over
items.detail: Production prove-out; old panels retained until stable.

items.title: Decommission relays
items.detail: Only after the PLC earns trust.

blocks.heading: The ask
items: Approve engineering hours to produce a firm quote (not this example band).
Reserve two weekend windows on the production calendar.
Assign a maintenance owner and an operations owner for cutover criteria.
Require a rollback plan in writing before the first wire moves.

blocks.quote: We are not replacing relays because they are old. We are replacing a failure mode we can no longer spare-parts our way out of.
blocks.attribution: The sentence to leave on the table

columns.name: Do nothing
columns.detail: EXAMPLE: keep paying intermittent downtime and last-time-buy premiums until a hard failure forces overtime rates.

columns.name: Refurbish relays in place
columns.detail: Buys months, not years, if the skus are already obsolete. Still leaves three undocumented brains.

columns.name: One PLC (this ask)
columns.detail: Central logic, named faults, staged cutover with rollback — higher upfront EXAMPLE cost, lower archaeological risk.

blocks.heading: Success criteria for the capital ask

items.label: Firm quote within EXAMPLE band or explained variance
Two documented weekend windows with rollback drills
Training complete for A and B shift techs before decommission
items.detail: HMI navigation and fault trees practiced.

items.label: Old panels retained until 30 stable production days

blocks.heading: Pitch discipline check
blocks.prompt: A manager asks if the $2,500/h downtime figure is guaranteed. Best reply?
options: It is an EXAMPLE — we will substitute historian-measured rates before capital approval
Ignore the question and talk about HMI colors
Triple the number to be safe
blocks.explanation: This page labels dollars as examples on purpose. Credibility is the pitch.
blocks.correctFeedback: Yes — keep examples labeled; bring real data next.
blocks.wrongFeedback: Re-read the warning callout. Example numbers are scaffolding, not scripture.

blocks.heading: Next step
blocks.body: If the manager nods, schedule the survey week. If they hesitate, leave the EXAMPLE ROI model and the obsolete-parts lead times — those two pages argue while you are gone.
